doc.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Chicago childhood: theaters, violin and first bass
title: Walter Barnes's band and the Chicago scene around 1929
summary: Hinton recalls Walter Barnes, a Vicksburg clarinetist whose band played the Al Capone Cotton Club, and the 1929 shift in Chicago music.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Yeah. I remember later in Chicago, one the big bands that came out of that era was the Walter Barnes band. Walter Barnes was from Vicksburg, Mississippi. In fact he went to my mother… he was a boyfriend of my mother‟s youngest sister and he was the one… I‟ve got some wonderful tapes here on Ed Birch. Ed Birch, he passed a couple of years ago, and we grew up together like brothers and I talked to him about this whole era. He worked in Walter Barnes‟ band at the Cotton Club when Al Capone opened the Cotton Club with Cicero. So I have some wonderful tapes on him talking… telling about that.
What kind of music did Walter Barnes play?
It was popular tunes of the day, jazz and things. There might be some records around here of Walter Barnes. He played clarinet, not a good clarinet; Ted Lewis type of thing that he played.
So he played like popular of the day?
Popular of the day, yeah, popular things, Donna Miller.
When those guys played did they sound like say Ted Lewis or did they sound like black bands?
Yeah. So they had something else going on rhythmically?
Yeah, a completed rhythm, like in Ted… the guy‟s saying the drummer‟s name and all the guys that played in the band because I‟m 15, 16, 17 years old.
So you know what‟s going on.
I know what‟s going on because that‟s 1929 and that‟s when the revolution started in Chicago as far as musical revolution. It changed the whole scene of the south side.
